messages.content: What is the freezing point point of water at a pressure of 10 kPa?

message.content:
At 10 kPa the equilibrium between liquid water and ice lies just below the normal‑temperature freezing point.  
Using the Clausius–Clapeyron relation for the solid–liquid transition (ΔS≈210 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, ΔV≈1×10⁻³ m³ mol⁻¹) gives a slope of roughly 0.21 MPa K⁻¹.  
Relative to atmospheric pressure (101.3 kPa) the drop of 91.3 kPa corresponds to a temperature shift of  

\[
\Delta T \approx \frac{0.0913\;\text{MPa}}{0.21\;\text{MPa K}^{-1}}\approx 0.44\;\text{K},
\]

so the freezing point falls by about 0.44 °C.  
Hence the freezing point of pure water at 10 kPa is **≈ −0.4 °C** (roughly –0.5 °C).  

(Values quoted in standard phase‑diagram tables give −0.43 °C at 10 kPa.)
